History & Physical (Super Detailed)

Consult Summary:
Adult male with 3-day history of frequent watery diarrhoea, intermittent left-lower-abdominal cramping, initial vomiting, and subjective fever after eating takeaway; clinical picture most consistent with acute gastroenteritis—viral most likely.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Loose, watery stools 6–7 times/day for the past 3 days.  
• Onset/progression: Began abruptly ~24 h after eating Chinese takeaway 4 days ago; frequency and looseness persistent, not improving yet.  
• Abdominal pain: Intermittent cramp-like pain in left lower abdomen; non-radiating; comes and goes.  
• Associated symptoms:  
  – Initial vomiting on day 1 (food contents, no blood), now resolved.  
  – Subjective fever at onset (felt hot but no recorded temperature).  
  – Weakness/shakiness, mild lethargy.  
  – Loss of appetite; tolerating oral fluids (soups, smoothies).  
  – No blood or mucus in stool; no melena; no persistent vomiting; no night sweats.  
• Exacerbating/relieving factors: Not specified; staying near toilet for convenience.  
• Impact on life: Difficulty attending work (accountant) due to toilet urgency.  
• Review of systems (pertinent negatives): No prior bowel problems, no urinary symptoms, no respiratory symptoms beyond controlled asthma, no trauma.

Past Medical History:
• Asthma – well-controlled with inhaler; no recent exacerbations.  
• No other chronic illnesses reported.  
• Medications: Salbutamol (or other) inhaler – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• Allergies: Not stated (missing).

Social History:
• Lives with wife and two children.  
• One child had transient vomiting but no diarrhoea.  
• Occupation: Accountant; has continued working despite symptoms.  
• Smoking: Never smoker.  
• Alcohol: Denies alcohol use.  
• Recreational drugs: Not discussed.

Family History:
• Not discussed.

Physical Examination:
(No in-person exam performed during telephone consult; no vitals available.)

Investigations:
• None performed to date.  
• Possible future stool culture if symptoms persist >3–4 days (per plan).

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1: Acute gastroenteritis (likely viral; bacterial food-borne infection also possible)  
  • Advice: Conservative management—maintain hydration with water and oral rehydration solution (e.g., Dioralyte).  
  • Medications: Paracetamol 2 tablets up to 4 ×/day as needed for fever/aches (exact strength not documented).  
  • Activity: Recommend 2–3 days off work for rest and to limit spread.  
  • Follow-up: Re-evaluate if no improvement in 3–4 days, worsening symptoms, inability to keep fluids down, or blood in stool/vomit.  
  • Contingency: If persists, arrange stool sample, consider further labs and targeted therapy (e.g., antibiotics if bacterial pathogen identified).

Issue 2: Asthma – stable  
  • Continue usual inhaler therapy; no changes required.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Acute viral gastroenteritis – High likelihood: matches abrupt onset after exposure, watery diarrhoea, vomiting, mild household spread, self-limiting course.  
2. Acute bacterial food-borne infection (Salmonella/Campylobacter/ETEC) – Moderate likelihood: temporal link to takeaway, abdominal cramps and subjective fever; absence of blood and lack of illness in co-diners makes less likely.  
3. Diverticulitis with secondary diarrhoea – Low–moderate likelihood: left-sided pain and low-grade systemic symptoms fit, but age unknown (< typical), predominant watery stool and lack of constant pain make this less probable.

Quality checks:
● Missing but expected: Allergies, detailed medication list (names/doses), baseline vitals, complete review of systems.  
● Conflicts: None noted between transcript and DDx.  
● Transcript quality: Clear; minor filler words but clinically adequate; no inaudible sections.
